figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Overview of FVQ. During quantizer training, multiple dense projections produce complementary views of the same visual feature, which are quantized in parallel by independent codebooks. The selected codewords are combined through tight-frame synthesis for feature reconstruction. In the subsequent VLM training stage, the quantizer is frozen, and only the resulting discrete indices are mapped to newly initialized token embeddings for multimodal understanding. The nine-metric average is computed over MMMU, MathVista, MMStar, OCRBench/10, ChartQA, CharXiv-DQ, CharXiv-RQ, DocVQA, and InfoVQA.

abstract: Discrete visual tokens represent vision in a discrete form analogous to language, offering a native interface for multimodal modeling under a shared next-token prediction objective. However, quantization error is widely assumed to cause unavoidable semantic loss, fundamentally limiting the semantic fidelity of discrete visual tokens and positioning continuous visual representations as an intrinsic upper bound. Using multimodal understanding as a proxy for semantic fidelity, we revisit this assumption and find quantization error unreliable, as discrete representations with substantially larger errors can achieve better understanding. Instead, the effective bit budget of discrete indices emerges as a key determinant of downstream performance. However, existing quantizers eventually saturate as additional codebooks contribute progressively less semantic information. As one approach to alleviating this saturation, we introduce Factorized Vector Quantization (FVQ), which quantizes complementary, fixed-dimensional views of the visual feature with symmetric parallel codebooks. It continues to improve at larger bit budgets, ultimately matching continuous visual representations in multimodal understanding. Trained on industrial-scale multimodal data, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance among discrete-representation models, outperforming UniAR and Emu3-Chat by 22.8% and 59.2%, respectively, on a nine-metric average. To our knowledge, it is also the first discrete-representation model competitive with strong continuous-representation models such as Qwen3-VL, including on fine-grained OCR tasks. We further identify the key principles and a practical recipe enabling this competitiveness. Together, these results and insights support the potential of discrete visual representations to underpin large-scale native multimodal foundation models.

sections.body: The introduction argues that quantization error is widely assumed to cause semantic loss, and it uses multimodal understanding as a proxy for semantic fidelity. The authors report that a discrete representation with an order-of-magnitude larger quantization error achieves substantially better understanding. The bit budget $B=L\log_{2}C$ grows linearly with the number of codebooks, and scaling it gives steady improvements in understanding (Fig. 1(a)). Factorized Vector Quantization (FVQ) keeps improving after residual and product quantization saturate. The paper reports relative gains of 22.8% over UniAR and 59.2% over Emu3-Chat on a nine-metric average, and competitiveness with flagship models such as Qwen3-VL.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Discrete visual tokens may reach continuous-level understanding at large bit budgets, motivating Factorized Vector Quantization.

sections.body: The analysis uses discrete QwenViT features. In Table 1, single-codebook vector quantization has feature-reconstruction MSE 0.027 and an average of 51.2. The odd-group residual variant has MSE 0.246 yet averages 60.7, and the even-group variant has MSE 0.028 and averages 59.3, so reconstruction error does not set semantic fidelity. The text reports that residual and product quantizers saturate at high budgets, and that going from 8 to 16 codebooks doubles the nominal bit budget but yields only marginal gains. The authors attribute this saturation to diminishing information per codebook, presented as an interpretation rather than a measured result.
sections.heading: What Determines the Semantics of Discrete Visual Representations?
sections.headline: Reconstruction error does not determine multimodal understanding, and existing residual and product quantizers saturate as the bit budget grows.

sections.body: FVQ gives each codebook a dense projection of the full feature to a fixed dimension, so the view any codebook receives does not shrink as codebooks are added. The stacked projections are constrained to a tight frame, $\mathbf{A}^{\top}\mathbf{A}=\rho\mathbf{I}_{D}$, which scales all feature directions equally so that no direction is discarded by all views at once. Each view is quantized independently and in parallel, so no codebook depends on another's residual, unlike residual vector quantization. Synthesis with the scaled transpose recovers the feature exactly before quantization, so all distortion comes from replacing views with their nearest codewords. The projections stay fixed during training and are built from a QR decomposition of a Gaussian matrix.
sections.heading: From Bit-Budget Scaling to Quantizer Design
sections.headline: Factorized Vector Quantization gives each codebook a fixed-dimensional dense view and recovers the feature exactly before quantization.

sections.body: Table 2 compares discrete quantizers with the continuous Qwen3 ViT representation under identical VLM training and evaluation settings. Residual vector quantization gives an average of 64.0 at both 8 and 16 codebooks, and product quantization reaches 64.3 at 16. FVQ reaches 65.3 at 16 codebooks, against 64.6 for continuous QwenViT. Table 3 reports that the main model, which pairs Qwen3-8B with 16-codebook FVQ, matches Qwen3-VL-8B on MathVista and achieves the best RealWorldQA result among the compared models. The main model is trained on industrial-scale data of 100B, 10B, 60B and 30B tokens across four stages.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Under identical settings, FVQ with 16 codebooks reaches 65.3 average against 64.6 for continuous QwenViT on eight benchmarks.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes that feature reconstruction error does not reliably predict downstream understanding, and that effective bit budget is a key determinant of semantic capacity. It states that existing multi-codebook quantizers saturate, and that FVQ is presented as one approach to alleviating this bottleneck. The industrial-scale model is reported to achieve the best performance among discrete-representation models and to remain competitive with continuous-representation models, including on fine-grained OCR and document understanding. The authors describe these results as support for discrete tokens as a scalable interface.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Results support discrete tokens as a scalable interface for native multimodal models, with FVQ offered as one approach to saturation.

sections.body:
- Quantizer training: nearest-neighbor quantization of frozen Vision Foundation Model features, with feature reconstruction, codebook and commitment losses.
- FVQ derivation: fixed dense projections, the tight-frame constraint, QR-based construction, parallel quantization, and exact synthesis before quantization.
- Related work on quantized visual encoders.
- Training stages, learning rates and token counts, with AdamW settings.
- Quantization position: 16× with merger reaches an average of 63.9, and 32× with Pre-Buffer reaches 63.5, so the text states Pre-Buffer is not essential.
- Figures 5–9, which are manually selected examples and not statistical evidence.
